To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the prevalence of bone destruction in the permanent dentition was high in English children aged initially 12 years; 2) the prevalence increased over a 3-year follow-up period; 3) the rate of bone destruction was higher in children who had bone destruction at baseline than in those who did not; and 4) bone destruction occurred at sites where there had been no evidence of disease at baseline.

18.5 percent of the children had bone loss at the initial examination, and 44 percent had bone loss at 3 years; the prevalence was higher for the children who had all second molars and first premolars fully erupted and present.
